questions.question: Why does adding threads usually NOT speed up CPU-bound pure-Python code in standard CPython?
options: Threads are disabled by default in CPython
The GIL allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time per process
Threads always run on a single CPU core due to the operating system
Python threads are actually separate processes
questions.explanation: The Global Interpreter Lock serialises bytecode execution, so CPU-bound threads just take turns. Threads still help I/O-bound work because the GIL is released while waiting.

questions.question: Which statement about Python 3.13's free-threaded build is accurate?
options: It removed the GIL for all Python installations
It is the default interpreter from 3.13 onward
It is an optional, experimental separate build with the GIL disabled
questions.explanation: PEP 703's free-threaded build (python3.13t) is optional and experimental; the default CPython build still has the GIL.

questions.question: What does `asyncio.gather(fetch(1), fetch(2), fetch(3))` return when awaited?
options: A list of results in the same order as the arguments
A list of results in the order the coroutines finished
Only the result of the first coroutine to finish
A set of Future objects that must be awaited individually
questions.explanation: gather runs the awaitables concurrently and returns their results in argument order, regardless of completion order.

questions.question: You need to resize 10,000 images using a pure-Python algorithm and want to use all CPU cores. What is the best fit?
options: A single thread with time.sleep between images
questions.explanation: CPU-bound work needs separate processes, each with its own interpreter and GIL, to achieve true parallelism.
